Arthritis is a medical condition in which one or more joints in the body become inflamed, causing pain, swelling, stiffness, and reduced ability to move.
Understanding the Key Word: "Joint"

Before going further, it helps to understand what a joint is. A joint is any place in your body where two bones meet and allow movement — like your knees, hips, fingers, wrists, shoulders, and ankles. Healthy joints have a smooth, rubbery layer called cartilage that cushions the bones and lets them glide past each other without friction. They are also surrounded by a thin lining called the synovial membrane, which produces a lubricating fluid to keep the joint moving smoothly.

When someone has arthritis, this smooth system breaks down — the joint becomes inflamed, damaged, or worn out — and movement becomes painful.
What Arthritis Feels Like

The most common signs of arthritis are:

  • Pain in the joint, which may be mild or severe
  • Swelling around the joint (it may look puffy or feel warm to the touch)
  • Stiffness, especially in the morning or after sitting still for a long time
  • Reduced range of motion — difficulty bending the knee fully, making a fist, or rotating the shoulder
  • Redness or warmth in the skin over the joint (in some types)

These symptoms can come and go, or they can be constant. In severe cases, arthritis can deform the joint — changing its shape permanently and making everyday tasks like opening a jar, climbing stairs, or walking very difficult.
Types of Arthritis

"Arthritis" is actually an umbrella term — it refers to over 100 different conditions, all involving joint inflammation or joint damage. However, a few types are the most important to know:

1. Osteoarthritis (OA)
This is the most common type. It is often called "wear-and-tear" arthritis. Over time — especially with age, heavy use, or injury — the cartilage that cushions the bones gradually wears away. When the cartilage thins or disappears, the bones begin to rub against each other, causing pain and stiffness. It most commonly affects the knees, hips, hands, and spine. It is a mechanical problem: the joint is physically breaking down.

2. Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
This is an autoimmune disease. In a healthy immune system, your body attacks germs and foreign threats. In rheumatoid arthritis, the immune system mistakenly attacks the body's own joint lining (the synovial membrane). This causes chronic inflammation that can damage the cartilage and bone over time. Unlike osteoarthritis, it often affects both sides of the body symmetrically (e.g., both wrists at the same time) and can also affect other organs like the eyes, lungs, and heart. It is a disease of the immune system, not just physical wear.

3. Psoriatic Arthritis
This type occurs in some people who have psoriasis (a skin condition that causes red, scaly patches). Their immune system's attack on the skin also affects the joints, causing arthritis.

4. Gout
Gout is caused by the buildup of a substance called uric acid in the blood. When uric acid levels get too high, it forms sharp, needle-like crystals that deposit inside joints — most commonly the big toe. This causes sudden, intense attacks of pain, swelling, and redness. Gout is often triggered by certain foods (like red meat, shellfish, and alcohol).

5. Septic Arthritis (Infectious Arthritis)
This occurs when a bacteria, virus, or fungus infects a joint directly. The infection causes rapid, severe inflammation. It is a medical emergency because if untreated, the infection can destroy the joint quickly.

6. Juvenile Arthritis
This refers to arthritis that develops in children (under 16 years old). The most common form is juvenile idiopathic arthritis. It is an autoimmune condition.
Who Gets Arthritis?

Arthritis can affect anyone — men, women, children, and the elderly — but some factors increase the risk:

  • Age: The older you get, the more likely your joints are to wear down (especially for osteoarthritis).
  • Sex: Women are more likely to develop rheumatoid arthritis; men are more prone to gout.
  • Genetics: Arthritis can run in families. If your parents had it, your risk is higher.
  • Obesity: Excess body weight puts extra stress on joints — particularly the knees, hips, and spine — accelerating cartilage damage.
  • Previous joint injuries: A joint that was injured in the past (from sports, accidents, or surgery) is more likely to develop arthritis later.
  • Occupation: Jobs that involve repetitive movements or heavy lifting (e.g., construction, farming) put joints under sustained stress and raise the risk.
  • Smoking: Associated with increased risk of rheumatoid arthritis.
What Causes Arthritis?

The cause depends on the type:

  • Osteoarthritis is caused by gradual mechanical wear and tear, aging, injury, or overuse.
  • Rheumatoid arthritis is caused by an abnormal immune response — the exact trigger is unknown, but genetics and environmental factors (like smoking) seem to play a role.
  • Gout is caused by excess uric acid, often from diet or kidney problems.
  • Septic arthritis is caused by infection.

In many cases — especially autoimmune types — the full cause remains only partially understood.
How Is It Diagnosed?

Doctors diagnose arthritis by combining several approaches:

  • Medical history and symptoms: The doctor asks about pain, stiffness, swelling, and when symptoms occur.
  • Physical examination: The doctor feels the joint, checks for swelling, warmth, tenderness, and range of motion.
  • Blood tests: These can detect markers of inflammation (like CRP or ESR), the rheumatoid factor (a protein linked to RA), uric acid levels (for gout), or antibodies (like anti-CCP for RA).
  • Imaging: X-rays reveal bone damage and joint space narrowing. MRI scans show soft tissue (cartilage, tendons, ligaments) in more detail. Ultrasound can detect inflammation in the joint lining.
  • Joint fluid analysis: In some cases, a doctor uses a needle to withdraw fluid from the joint and examines it under a microscope — this is especially useful for diagnosing gout (crystals are visible) or septic arthritis (bacteria may be found).
Can Arthritis Be Cured?

For most types, no — there is no complete cure. However, it can be managed very effectively.

  • Osteoarthritis cannot be reversed, but its progression can be slowed and symptoms controlled.
  • Rheumatoid arthritis is a lifelong disease, but modern medications can achieve remission (a state where the disease is suppressed and causes little or no damage).
  • Gout can be fully controlled and attacks prevented with the right diet and medication.
  • Septic arthritis can be cured with antibiotics or antifungal treatment, though the joint may retain some damage.
How Is Arthritis Treated?

Treatment is tailored to the type and severity. The main approaches are:

Medications:

  • Pain relievers (like paracetamol/acetaminophen) for mild pain.
  • NSAIDs (non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, like ibuprofen or naproxen) reduce both pain and inflammation.
  • Corticosteroids (like prednisone) are powerful anti-inflammatory drugs used for flare-ups.
  • DMARDs (Disease-Modifying Antirheumatic Drugs, like methotrexate) slow the progression of autoimmune types like RA by suppressing the immune system.
  • Biologics are a newer, advanced class of drugs that target specific parts of the immune system to reduce inflammation in RA and similar conditions.
  • Uric-acid-lowering drugs (like allopurinol) prevent gout attacks.

Physical and occupational therapy:
Exercises that strengthen the muscles around the joint, improve flexibility, and reduce load on the joint. Occupational therapists can suggest tools and techniques that make daily tasks easier and less painful.

Lifestyle changes:

  • Weight loss (reduces strain on joints)
  • Low-impact exercise like swimming or cycling (keeps joints mobile without harsh impact)
  • Hot and cold therapy (heat relaxes muscles; cold reduces swelling)
  • Eating a healthy diet (especially for gout — avoiding high-purine foods)

Surgery (for severe cases):

  • Joint replacement: The damaged joint is replaced with an artificial one made of metal, plastic, or ceramic. Hip and knee replacements are among the most common and successful surgeries in medicine.
  • Joint fusion (arthrodesis): Two bones are fused together to eliminate the painful joint. This eliminates movement but removes pain.
Is Arthritis Serious?

It varies greatly. Mild arthritis may cause occasional discomfort but little interference with daily life. Severe, untreated arthritis — particularly autoimmune types — can be debilitating, permanently deforming joints and affecting the ability to work, move, and care for oneself. Systemic types like RA can also affect other organs and increase the risk of heart disease. Early diagnosis and treatment are therefore important.
In Summary

Arthritis is an umbrella term for conditions in which joints become inflamed or damaged, causing pain, swelling, stiffness, and loss of movement. The most common types are osteoarthritis (physical wear and tear), rheumatoid arthritis (immune system attacking the joint), and gout (uric acid crystals in the joint). It affects people of all ages, though it is more common with age. While most forms cannot be cured, they can be managed effectively through medication, therapy, lifestyle changes, and sometimes surgery.
